desc:
Choose exactly k elements of nums such that no two chosen elements are next to each other (indices i and i + 1 never both chosen). Return the largest possible sum of the chosen values.

Values may be negative, so you cannot simply skip bad elements: you must still reach exactly k picks. The input always allows a valid choice.

For example, for nums = [4, -1, 5, -2, 3] and k = 2 the answer is 9 (take 4 and 5), and for k = 3 it is 12 (take 4, 5 and 3).
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ ceil(nums.length / 2), so a valid choice always exists
hints: The plain House Robber DP has one dimension. Because the number of picks matters now, what extra information must the state carry?
Let f[i][j] be the best sum using only the first i elements with exactly j picks. Either the last element is skipped, or it is picked and the previous pick lies at index i-2 or earlier.
f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i-2][j-1] + nums[i-1]). Mark impossible states with a very negative value. Only rows i-1 and i-2 are needed, so keep two rolling arrays of length k + 1.
editorial: Add the pick count to the state. With f[i][j] = best sum from the first i elements using exactly j picks (and -infinity when impossible), the last element is either unused, giving f[i-1][j], or used, in which case its left neighbour is unused and the other j-1 picks come from the first i-2 elements, giving f[i-2][j-1] + nums[i-1]. The base state is f[i][0] = 0.

The answer is f[n][k]; the constraint on k guarantees it is reachable. Each row depends only on the two rows before it, so two arrays of size k + 1 suffice, and j never needs to exceed (i + 1) / 2. Time O(n · k), space O(k). A greedy 'take the largest and fix up' idea fails because a big element can block two good neighbours.
